rationale.standard_ref: Cisco hierarchical campus design; Project rule
rationale.text: Campus: collapsed-core design (core and distribution combined) because the site has 3 building(s), below the 4-building point where a separate distribution layer pays off. Fewer devices and hops for 1600 endpoints.
BldgA: 650 access ports needed, so 14 × 48-port switch(es) in 2 stack(s) (≤ 8 members per stack). 22 spare port(s) are shut down.
BLDGA-ACC2: 140 PoE port(s) × 30.0 W (802.3at Type 2) = 4200.0 W of PoE budget required from the switch power supplies.
BldgB: 510 access ports needed, so 11 × 48-port switch(es) in 2 stack(s) (≤ 8 members per stack). 18 spare port(s) are shut down.
BLDGB-ACC2: 110 PoE port(s) × 30.0 W (802.3at Type 2) = 3300.0 W of PoE budget required from the switch power supplies.
BldgC: 440 access ports needed, so 10 × 48-port switch(es) in 2 stack(s) (≤ 8 members per stack). 40 spare port(s) are shut down.
BLDGC-ACC2: 40 PoE port(s) × 30.0 W (802.3at Type 2) = 1200.0 W of PoE budget required from the switch power supplies.
Campus: resiliency is high, so core switches are paired and every access stack is dual-homed to both gateways. Any single device or uplink can fail without isolating users.
Native VLAN is the unused VLAN 999 on every trunk (not VLAN 1) and it is left out of the allowed lists. This blocks double-tagging VLAN hopping. Unused access ports are parked in it and shut down.
Access ports use PortFast (RSTP edge port, forwards immediately) and BPDU Guard (err-disables the port if a switch is plugged in), preventing accidental loops.
Campus: VLANs 10,11,12,20,21,30,40,41,42,50 each carry one segment, giving each role its own broadcast domain.
BLDGA-ACC1 trunk to CAMPUS-CORE1 allows only VLANs 10, the VLANs that have ports behind it, instead of all 4094. This limits broadcast flooding and blast radius.
BLDGA-ACC1 trunk to CAMPUS-CORE2 allows only VLANs 10, the VLANs that have ports behind it, instead of all 4094. This limits broadcast flooding and blast radius.
BLDGA-ACC2 trunk to CAMPUS-CORE1 allows only VLANs 10,20,40,50, the VLANs that have ports behind it, instead of all 4094. This limits broadcast flooding and blast radius.
BLDGA-ACC2 trunk to CAMPUS-CORE2 allows only VLANs 10,20,40,50, the VLANs that have ports behind it, instead of all 4094. This limits broadcast flooding and blast radius.
BLDGB-ACC1 trunk to CAMPUS-CORE1 allows only VLANs 11, the VLANs that have ports behind it, instead of all 4094. This limits broadcast flooding and blast radius.
BLDGB-ACC1 trunk to CAMPUS-CORE2 allows only VLANs 11, the VLANs that have ports behind it, instead of all 4094. This limits broadcast flooding and blast radius.
BLDGB-ACC2 trunk to CAMPUS-CORE1 allows only VLANs 11,21,41, the VLANs that have ports behind it, instead of all 4094. This limits broadcast flooding and blast radius.
BLDGB-ACC2 trunk to CAMPUS-CORE2 allows only VLANs 11,21,41, the VLANs that have ports behind it, instead of all 4094. This limits broadcast flooding and blast radius.
BLDGC-ACC1 trunk to CAMPUS-CORE1 allows only VLANs 12, the VLANs that have ports behind it, instead of all 4094. This limits broadcast flooding and blast radius.
BLDGC-ACC1 trunk to CAMPUS-CORE2 allows only VLANs 12, the VLANs that have ports behind it, instead of all 4094. This limits broadcast flooding and blast radius.
BLDGC-ACC2 trunk to CAMPUS-CORE1 allows only VLANs 12,30,42, the VLANs that have ports behind it, instead of all 4094. This limits broadcast flooding and blast radius.
BLDGC-ACC2 trunk to CAMPUS-CORE2 allows only VLANs 12,30,42, the VLANs that have ports behind it, instead of all 4094. This limits broadcast flooding and blast radius.
Campus: Rapid PVST+ root primary on CAMPUS-CORE1 and secondary on CAMPUS-CORE2, so the root bridge is also the default gateway and frames never take a detour through an access switch.

Campus: HSRPv2 gives each VLAN a virtual gateway (first usable address) shared by CAMPUS-CORE1 (priority 110, active) and CAMPUS-CORE2 (priority 100, standby). Each subnet reserves 2 extra addresses for the physical SVIs.
Single-area OSPF (area 0) because the design is one site with 13 subnets, below the 50-subnet threshold. One link-state database converges fast and needs no ABRs.
Staff-A: 452 hosts + 1 gateway need 453 usable addresses; the smallest block is /23 (2^9 − 2 = 510 usable), giving 88.82% utilization.
Staff-B: 402 hosts + 1 gateway need 403 usable addresses; the smallest block is /23 (2^9 − 2 = 510 usable), giving 79.02% utilization.
Staff-C: 302 hosts + 1 gateway need 303 usable addresses; the smallest block is /23 (2^9 − 2 = 510 usable), giving 59.41% utilization.
Guest-C: 102 hosts + 1 gateway need 103 usable addresses; the smallest block is /25 (2^7 − 2 = 126 usable), giving 81.75% utilization.
Servers: 62 hosts + 1 gateway need 63 usable addresses; the smallest block is /25 (2^7 − 2 = 126 usable), giving 50.0% utilization.
Voice-A: 102 hosts + 1 gateway need 103 usable addresses; the smallest block is /25 (2^7 − 2 = 126 usable), giving 81.75% utilization.
Voice-B: 82 hosts + 1 gateway need 83 usable addresses; the smallest block is /25 (2^7 − 2 = 126 usable), giving 65.87% utilization.
APs-A: 42 hosts + 1 gateway need 43 usable addresses; the smallest block is /26 (2^6 − 2 = 62 usable), giving 69.35% utilization.
APs-B: 32 hosts + 1 gateway need 33 usable addresses; the smallest block is /26 (2^6 − 2 = 62 usable), giving 53.23% utilization.
APs-C: 42 hosts + 1 gateway need 43 usable addresses; the smallest block is /26 (2^6 − 2 = 62 usable), giving 69.35% utilization.
CAMPUS-CORE1--CAMPUS-CORE2: point-to-point link gets a /31 (RFC 3021): both addresses are usable, so no network/broadcast addresses are wasted as a /30 would.
CAMPUS-CORE1 Loopback0: loopback gets a /32, a single stable address used as the router ID.
CAMPUS-CORE2 Loopback0: loopback gets a /32, a single stable address used as the router ID.

Allocated 2244 of 65536 addresses in 10.10.0.0/16 (3.42% of the root used). 1634 addresses were actually needed, so packing efficiency is 72.82% (610 addresses lost to power-of-two rounding). Blocks were allocated largest-first, so each block starts on its natural boundary and none overlap.
Area 0 is OSPF area 0 with address block 10.10.0.0/16.
Router IDs come from Loopback0 /32 addresses. A loopback never goes down with a physical interface, so OSPF and BGP identities stay stable.
OSPF reference bandwidth is 100000 Mbps. With the default 100 Mbps every link of 100 Mb/s or more gets cost 1, so 10G and 1G paths would look equal.
Guest-C → Servers: deny ip via ACL-GUEST-C-IN, applied inbound on the Guest-C gateway so the decision is made at the first layer-3 hop.
Guest-C → Staff-A: deny ip via ACL-GUEST-C-IN, applied inbound on the Guest-C gateway so the decision is made at the first layer-3 hop.
Guest-C → Staff-B: deny ip via ACL-GUEST-C-IN, applied inbound on the Guest-C gateway so the decision is made at the first layer-3 hop.
Guest-C → Staff-C: deny ip via ACL-GUEST-C-IN, applied inbound on the Guest-C gateway so the decision is made at the first layer-3 hop.
ACL-GUEST-C-IN ends with 'permit ip any any' so traffic not covered by a policy is allowed; otherwise the IOS implicit deny would drop all other traffic from Guest-C.
6 in-building connection(s) (switch-to-switch and router-to-switch in the same building) are patch runs assumed ≤ 100 m, so Cat6a 10GBASE-T is used.
